title: HMRC Business Mileage Rates: What Contractors Can Actually Claim

html:
You drive to a client site every week, log the miles, and assume you can claim them. But if you have been going to the same place for more than 24 months, HMRC may disagree.

Mileage claims are one of the most valuable tax reliefs available to contractors and freelancers who drive for work. The problem is that most guides stop at the rate table. They tell you the number but not whether your journeys actually qualify, how to process the claim correctly depending on your business structure, or what records will protect you if HMRC ever asks questions.

This article gives you the current 2026/27 HMRC approved mileage rates, the commuting and 24-month rules explained in plain terms, and a clear record-keeping checklist you can use today. Whether you operate through a limited company or as a sole trader, you will know exactly what to claim and how to claim it correctly.

The current HMRC business mileage rates for 2026/27

HMRC sets Approved Mileage Allowance Payments (AMAPs) as the maximum rate you can be reimbursed tax-free for using your own vehicle for business travel. From April 2026, the rate for cars and vans increased to 55p per mile for the first 10,000 business miles in a tax year. After that threshold, the rate drops to 25p per mile. The Autumn Budget on 28 October 2026 made the 55p rate permanent and raises the rate above 10,000 miles to 35p from 6 April 2027.

This is the first increase since 2011, when the rate moved from 40p to 45p. The April 2026 uplift to 55p reflects the rising cost of fuel, insurance, and vehicle running costs that contractors have absorbed for over a decade.

Vehicle typeFirst 10,000 milesAbove 10,000 miles
Cars and vans55p per mile25p per mile (35p from 6 April 2027)
Motorcycles24p per mile24p per mile
Bicycles20p per mile20p per mile

There is also a passenger rate: if you carry a fellow employee in your vehicle on a business journey, you can claim an additional 5p per mile per passenger. This is separate from the main AMAP rate and is often overlooked entirely.

The full published rates are available directly from HMRC's travel mileage and fuel rates and allowances page.

What counts as a business journey, and what does not

Can I claim mileage for driving to the same client site every day?

This is the question that trips up the most contractors. The short answer is: it depends on how long you have been going there and whether it qualifies as a temporary workplace.

HMRC distinguishes between ordinary commuting and business travel. Ordinary commuting is travel between your home and a permanent workplace. That is never claimable, regardless of how far you drive. Business travel is travel to a temporary workplace, a client site, or any location that is not your regular base. That is claimable.

The 24-month temporary workplace rule: the trap that catches people out

What is the 24-month temporary workplace rule?

A workplace is only treated as temporary if you are not expected to work there for more than 24 months. Once you have worked at a location for 24 months, or you know from the outset that you will be there for longer than 24 months, HMRC reclassifies it as a permanent workplace. From that point, your travel there becomes ordinary commuting and is no longer claimable.

The rule applies from the moment you know the contract will exceed 24 months, not just after you have been there for two years. If you sign a 30-month contract on day one, your travel to that site is not claimable from day one.

If you are unsure whether your current contract puts you at risk, our tax planning for contractors guidance covers how to review your position before it becomes a problem.

For the full HMRC technical position on temporary workplaces, see HMRC's Employment Income Manual EIM32080.

How to claim mileage as a limited company director

How do I claim business mileage as a limited company director?

As a limited company director, you are both an employee and a shareholder of your company. This means the process for claiming mileage is different from a sole trader. You do not claim mileage on your personal Self Assessment return. Instead, your company reimburses you for the business miles you drive in your personal vehicle.

You can claim your mileage directly on FreeAgent, who calculate all the figures for you. If you are a VAT registered company, you can also reclaim the VAT on the petrol proportion of the mileage claim, just make sure to snap a photo of your petrol receipt when you fill up. Don't worry, FreeAgent handles all the calculations for you.

You can reimburse yourself for the mileage claims that you make. That reimbursement is tax-free for you and is a deductible expense for the company, reducing your Corporation Tax liability.

If you are just getting started with this structure, our guide to starting out as a contractor with a limited company covers the broader financial setup you need to get right from day one.

How to claim mileage as a sole trader

As a sole trader, you claim business mileage directly through your Self Assessment tax return. You record your total business miles for the year and apply HMRC's simplified mileage rates, which are the same 55p and 25p (35p above 10,000 miles from 6 April 2027). You can claim actual vehicle costs instead, but once you use the flat rate for a vehicle you must stick with it. The resulting figure is deducted from your taxable profit, reducing your Income Tax and National Insurance liability.

For sole traders approaching the Making Tax Digital threshold, accurate mileage records feed directly into your quarterly submissions. Getting the habit right now saves significant time when MTD becomes mandatory for your income band. Our guide to your taxes as a contractor explains how mileage fits into your wider tax picture.

What records HMRC expects you to keep

What records do I need to keep for a mileage claim?

HMRC does not prescribe a specific format, but they are clear about what information a mileage log must contain. For each journey, you need to record:

  • The date of the journey
  • The start and end location (or destination)
  • The business purpose of the journey
  • The number of miles travelled
  • A running total of business miles for the tax year

All of this information can be stored in your FreeAgent account, reducing the burden for spreadsheets and paper trails.
